headline: Kind Words
text: Kind words do not cost much. And they nevet blister the tongue or lips. And we have never heard Of any mental trouble arising from this quarter. Though they do not cost much, yet they accomplish much. They help ones good nature and good will. Soft words soften our own SOUL Angry words are fuel to fame of wrath, and make it blaze the more fercely. Kind words make other people good ma tured. Cold words freeze people, and hot words scOrch them, and bitter words make them biterer, and wrathful words make them wrahful. headline: The Indian Bsttle-Defeat Of the Sioux | Indians-5O0 Reported az Killed.
text: LOUISVILLE, August ia returned Californian, who had reached Independ- ence, gives the following account of the Indian battle, before reported, as having occurred between the Sioux and Pawnee Indians. The Sioux were aided in the war by the Cheyennes Indians. and the combined forces were about 5000 strong. The Pawnecs were assisted by the Iowas, Saxs and Pottawattomies, numbering in all about 5000. The opposing forces met about fifty miles from Fort Kearney, and the battle lasted all day, resulting in the loss on both sides of from five to six hundred killed. The Sioux party, though the most numerous, were defeated A person who has come in from Fort Laramie, says the above account is exag- gerated, but says that great demonstra- ton was made, and had not the Pottawat- omies interfered, the Pawnees would have been defeated. He thinks that hundreds, instead of thousands, would be nearer the mark, as to the actual numbers engaged, and the number killed was doubtless much exaggerated.

text: Terrible Explosion at the fremont Hotel, Galveston. GALVESTON, May ga terrible oatas trophe occurred in this city at $50 o'clock this morning. After causing this destruction, the giant missile finally landed Inside of an adjoining small structure, .protrudlng half inside the house ana half out. VARIOUS THEORIES are anoat in regard w. headline: A Genuinn Love Story Christian Advocate.
text: This story, told originally by Spur geon we believe, will, we are confident, strike chord in many loving hearts: A young clergyman and his bride were invited guests at large party given by wealthy parishioner. In all the freshness and elegance of her bridal wardrobe the young wife shone among the throng, distinguished by her come illness and vivacity and rich attire; and when during the evening, her young husband drew her aside and whispered to her that she was the most beautiful woman in all the company, and that his heart was bursting with pride and love for her, she thought herself the happiest wife in the world. Ten years later the same husband and wife were the guests at the same house, where was gathered a similar gay company. The wife of ten years ago wore the same dress she had worn on the previous occasion: and, OF course, 1t had been altered and re-made, and was old-fashioned and al most shabby. Toll and care and moth erhood and pinched circumstances had taken the roses out of her cheeks and the activity out of her form. She sat apart from the crowd, care-worn and preoc- cupied. Her small hands, roughened with coarse toll, were ungloved, for the minister's salary was painfully small. A little apart the ten-year husband stood and looked at his wife, and as he OBJ served her faded dress and weary atti- tude great sense of all her patient, loving faithfulness came over his heart. Looking up, she caught his earnest gaze, and noticed that his eyes were filled with tears. headline: Died After Long Illness.
text: Special to The Washington Herald. Richmond, Va, June g.-Miss Julia Ma gruder. the famous Virginia authoress, died late this afternoon az St Luke's Hospital, after an illness extending over several weeks. headline: RICH WAR HERO KILLED IN FIRST SOLO FLIGHT J. oliver Beebe, Boston Merchant, Plunged 400 Feet-His Two Children Watch.
text: BY the Associated Press. BOSTON, May 31.-J. Oliver Beebe, World War hero and wealthy Boston leather merchant, plunged 400 feet to his death yesterday in an airplane in which he was making his first solo flight. Several thousand persons, in Guiding Beebe's 9-year-old son and g. year-old daughter, witnessed the trag- edy which occurred about 100 yards from the East Boston airport. Beebe had been flying with an in structor, and just prior to his solo attempt had taken the children and nurse for flight Taking the controls himself, he made one perfect landing, and apparently was attempting to circle down for another when the cabin monoplane went into spin and buried itself in the mud flats. Beebe, who was 40 years old, was graduated from Harvard in 1915. and was cited for bravery by both the French and American governments dur ing his service as an ambulance driver in the World War;

headline: Secrecy Veil Lifted From 5pitsbergen
text: By lne ASSOclaleQ PreSs. LONDON, Sept. 13.-A veil of wartime secrecy was lifted today from the Arctic isle of Spitsbergen and the Norwegian government-in- exile told for the first time the story of small band of Norwegians who maintained a vital weather station there for year and half. The government disclosed that no word had been heard from the gar rison since it signaled the APPROACH of a German feet which Berlin announced had attacked and de- stroyed installations there last We'd nesday. Since May, 1912, the garrison, numbering fewer than 100 men, had manned the weather station and provided information needed for ships sailing the northern route to Russia. The last official news concerning the archipelago. only $50 miles be- low the North Pole, was announced in September, l941, when an Allied force evacuated all persons living there and destroyed coal mines which the Germans were reported using. Then tight censorship was clamped down. A month after the Allied landing, the Germans moved in. The fol- lowing May the Norwegians arrived to build an Allied weather station. German aircraft attacked the group daily. On July British naval force arrived, and the German gar rison slipped away. Since then, the Norwegians had been undisturbed until the German warships arrived.

ALLIED HEADQUARTERS Naples, Feb. ia fierce tank battle has broken the lull on the beachhead south of Rome, with the Germans launching heavy attacks in the Carroceto april la sector, 10 miles north oil Anzio, but all evidence today in dicated the Allied forces were holding against continuing enemy thrusts. An announcement at headquarters said the Germans struck yesterday morning after heavy artillery preparation. Both sides threw tanks into the heavy fighting. The Americans and British were said to be grimly holding to their positions in the face of tremendous pressure. 1t was the second all-out German attempt to smash the Allied beach, head. The Nazis were said to be throwing their full force of infan- try, tanks and artillery into the struggle, which was hourly increas- ing in violence. Nine NaZi Planes DOwned. Enemy aircraft swung into the battle in unusual force, some 100 sortles attacking objectives in the battle zone. But the Allied air forces met the air attack, blow for blow, shooting down nine of the attackers and blasting targets in the fighting area. The beachhead fighting far eclipsed that in strategic Casino, where American forces still were bitterly contesting the Nazi stranglehold house by house. RAF and Austria liam KittyhaWks again bombed the ruins of the Monte Casino Mon astery American planes hit Ger man positions elsewhere on Abbey Hill. In a day of extensive and wide ranging air activity Allied bombers, large and small, and fighters flew approximately 1000 sorties. The en- emy railway yards in Rome were hit for the second straight day and heavy and medium bombers attacked communicate tions at many points north of the Italian capital. Four Allied planes were lost. The sweeping air offensive COW cred Is main and secondary rail lines around Rome, Tanks Support Nazi Drive After the long and concentrated German artillery barrage yesterday morning the first enemy shock troops struck in the first phases of the new beachhead attack with tanks in sup port. The enemy attack around Car roceto came in an area where much of the previous heavy fighting had taken place. Various vantage points in the sector have changed hands several times. Carroceto itself was in German hands at latest report. The Germans opened the new offensive after apparently recovering from losses suffered in the first major effort to drive American and British troops into the sea, but dur ing the lull the Allies also had built up new strength and were ready for and expecting the assault. Because of the voluminous nature Of the report, the COM mittee will have to study it fur ther before taking action, SEN ator Carlson said. Among the proposals was one for a complete new Federal pay system for classified and postal employees. Somewhat along the line of the original Hoover Commission proposals on pay, the recommen- dation would set up a compen- sation board within the Civil Service Commission. Less atten- ton would be paid elaborate job descriptions as provided in the present Classification Act. Instead, pay would be based on the type of job and the pay Of comparable jobs in the local ity where a Federal worker was employed. Another factor would be the jobs Importance in the labor market where the employe worked. Congress would set the mini mum and maximum Federal pay rates, but the compensation board would set rates for all in dividual employees within the floor and ceiling and could adj just the salaries from time to time.
